title: Edge Compute & IoT Networking
blurb: Tests the edge-cloud split, choosing among MQTT, CoAP, BLE and LoRaWAN, MQTT QoS levels, quantization, pruning and distillation and what each really gives, inference runtimes, and why a cloud round trip misses a 20 ms control deadline most of the time.

refLinks.label: §64.2.3 Model Compression: Closing the Gap Between Training-Time and Deployment-Time Constraints

ideas.title: Runtimes and profiling on target hardware

questions.prompt: What decides whether a piece of computation must run on the device?
options: Whether the data is stored in the cloud already
Whether it is in the loop or must work offline
Whether the device has a GPU of any kind
Whether the model has more than a million parameters
questions.explanation: Anything inside the real-time loop, or that must survive a dropped connection, runs on-device. Fleet analytics and retraining can go to the cloud.

questions.prompt: Which of these belong in the cloud, per the chapter's split? Select all that apply.
options: Fleet-wide monitoring and dashboards
Retraining on aggregated fleet data
Safety-critical fallback behaviour
A/B testing across the fleet
questions.explanation: Safety fallbacks must work with no connectivity, so they run on the device. The other three can tolerate delay.

questions.prompt: A soil-moisture sensor sends one reading an hour across several kilometres on battery power. Which protocol fits?
options: BLE straight to the cloud
LoRaWAN, low power, long range
MQTT over WiFi
CoAP over Ethernet
questions.explanation: LoRaWAN gives kilometres of range at very low power, with low bandwidth that sparse telemetry doesn't mind.

options: Choosing CoAP for a device with only a few KB of RAM
Choosing LoRaWAN for sparse telemetry over long distances
Choosing BLE for a wearable that hands off to a phone
Choosing MQTT for a coin-cell sensor meant to last for years
questions.explanation: MQTT's TCP overhead drains a coin cell far faster than BLE or LoRaWAN. The other three are good fits.

questions.prompt: Which protocol suits the data inside a real-time control loop?
options: None. Control runs locally.
CoAP, since it uses UDP
LoRaWAN, for its long range
MQTT at QoS 2, for exactly-once delivery
questions.explanation: Procedure 64.1 says these protocols are for telemetry, configuration and coordination, not the loop itself.

options: At-least-once delivery, with retries
Fire-and-forget, with no guarantee at all
Delivery within a fixed time limit
Exactly-once delivery, with no duplicates
questions.explanation: QoS 0 is fire-and-forget, QoS 1 at-least-once, QoS 2 exactly-once. Occasional duplicates are usually harmless for sensor data.

questions.prompt: What does dynamic quantization reliably deliver?
options: A smaller model file, every time
Faster inference on every CPU
Higher accuracy than the original
A sparser weight matrix
questions.explanation: Fewer bits per weight shrinks size by construction. Speed is conditional and was negative in the worked example. Sparsity comes from pruning.

questions.prompt: Why may unstructured pruning give no speed-up?
options: Pruned weights are restored automatically at inference time.
Dense kernels gain nothing from scattered zeros.
Pruning always adds layers to make up for removed weights.
Pruning only reduces the model's accuracy, never its size.
questions.explanation: Speed-ups need a runtime that exploits sparsity, or structured pruning that removes whole channels.

questions.prompt: What does a distilled student learn from that plain training on labels misses?
options: The teacher's exact weights, copied layer by layer
The teacher's pruning mask
A larger dataset that the teacher generates
The teacher's full output distribution
questions.explanation: Soft outputs carry more signal than hard labels, the same idea as in Book 2.

questions.prompt: Post-training quantization costs more accuracy than you can accept. What does the chapter suggest?
options: Unstructured pruning instead, which keeps accuracy fixed
Quantization-aware training
Doubling the batch size during inference
Dynamic quantization, which never loses accuracy
questions.explanation: QAT simulates quantization during training. It costs retraining but has the smallest accuracy loss of the options.

questions.prompt: Why export a model to ONNX?
options: One export runs on many runtimes and hardware types.
ONNX is required by every NVIDIA Jetson device.
ONNX quantizes the model automatically on export.
ONNX models train faster than PyTorch models.
questions.explanation: ONNX Runtime is the portable option. TensorRT is NVIDIA-specific, and TFLite targets mobile.

questions.prompt: What does Procedure 64.5 require when profiling for a deployment decision? Select all that apply.
options: The full pipeline, not only the forward pass
A realistic batch size, usually 1 for control
The mean latency alone
Hardware of the same class as the target
questions.explanation: Mean latency alone is not enough. The procedure asks for a distribution (p50, p95, p99), since deadline misses depend on the tail.

questions.prompt: In the simulation, what share of cloud round trips missed the 20 ms deadline? Give a percentage to one decimal place.
questions.explanation: 79.3%, roughly four in five. On-device inference missed 0%.

questions.prompt: Why did the cloud path miss so often, even with a fast model?
options: The device sent requests faster than the cloud accepted.
The cloud server dropped most requests under load.
Network latency alone often exceeded the whole budget.
The cloud model was larger and slower than the device model.
questions.explanation: With a mean of 34 ms and p95 of 68 ms, the round trip blows a 20 ms budget before any compute happens.

questions.prompt: Quantization shrank the model from 284.6 KB to 76.6 KB. What percentage reduction is that? Give one decimal place.
Batch-1 latency rose by about 257% after quantization. Why?
options: Quantization doubled the number of layers.
The quantized model ran on a slower CPU core.
Per-call quantize overhead beat the tiny matmuls.
INT8 arithmetic is always slower than FP32.
questions.explanation: For a small model, the overhead dominates. Larger models or hardware with fast INT8 kernels see real gains.

questions.prompt: A teammate quantizes a model for an edge robot and reports it faster, from laptop tests at batch size 64. What does the chapter suggest?
options: Ship it, since quantization always speeds up inference.
Re-measure on target hardware at batch 1, with tails.
Skip testing, since size reduction proves speed.
Ship it, since batch 64 is a stricter test than batch 1.
questions.explanation: Batch-1 and batch-64 behaved differently here (+257% against +20%), and laptops differ from edge devices. Control loops care about single-sample tail latency.

bookExercises.prompt: State the deciding question this chapter uses to assign a piece of computation to the edge vs. the cloud, and apply it to (a) a robot's obstacle-avoidance check and (b) a monthly fleet-wide performance dashboard.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: The deciding question: can this decision tolerate the latency, reliability, and bandwidth cost of a cloud round-trip? (a) A robot's obstacle-avoidance check cannot. It's a time-critical control-loop decision that must run on the edge. (b) A monthly fleet-wide performance dashboard easily can. It's not time-critical and benefits from centralized aggregation, so it belongs in the cloud.

bookExercises.prompt: Name the three axes (power, range, bandwidth/latency) that IoT protocols trade off against each other, and explain why LoRaWAN sacrifices bandwidth to achieve its range.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: The three axes are power, range, and bandwidth/latency. LoRaWAN sacrifices bandwidth (very low) specifically to achieve long range (kilometres) at very low power. The radio physics trade-off is that transmitting reliably over long distances at low power requires a much narrower, slower signal than short-range high-bandwidth protocols like BLE use.

bookExercises.prompt: Using Listing 64.5's pattern, explain why a 73% size reduction with quantization is "essentially guaranteed by construction" while the latency change is not. What's structurally different about the two measurements?
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Quantization's size reduction follows directly from the arithmetic of storing fewer bits per weight (e.g. FP32 → INT8 is mechanically a 4x reduction before any measurement). It's essentially guaranteed by construction. Latency, by contrast, depends on whether the actual runtime and hardware have optimized kernels for the lower-precision operations; on a generic CPU without such optimized paths, INT8 operations can be *slower* than native FP32 paths, which is a property of the software/hardware stack, not of the arithmetic itself.

bookExercises.prompt: The Worked Example's on-device latency simulation uses the *quantized* model's measured latency (0.078ms) rather than the FP32 model's (0.022ms), even though quantization made this specific model slower. Explain why this is still the right choice for a real deployment decision, given this chapter's compression trade-offs discussion.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: A real deployment decision should be based on the actual on-device latency of the model that will actually run in production, which is the quantized model, since that's the one being deployed for its size benefit. Using the FP32 model's latency would answer a question ("how fast would the model I'm not shipping be") irrelevant to the real deployment; this chapter's own finding that quantization can make a model smaller *and* slower is exactly why the deployed model's own measured number, not an assumption transferred from a different model, is the only trustworthy figure.

bookExercises.prompt: A customer wants to run their perception model in the cloud "because the GPU is bigger there" for a robot with a 20ms control loop. Using this chapter's deadline-miss measurement (Listing 64.6), write the two or three sentences you'd say back, citing the specific numbers.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: "A cloud round-trip typically costs tens of milliseconds mean latency with a long tail, which this chapter's own measurement showed causes deadline misses against a 20ms control-loop budget. Running perception in the cloud for this robot would mean the decision routinely arrives after the control loop already needed it, which isn't a 'bigger GPU is better' trade-off, it's an outright miss."

bookExercises.prompt: A team pruned 40% of a CNN's weights and is disappointed inference didn't get any faster on their deployment hardware. Using Procedure 64.3, diagnose the likely cause and name the fix.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Likely cause (Procedure 64.3): unstructured pruning was used, and the deployment runtime doesn't exploit sparse weight structure. Per the compression comparison table, unstructured pruning's speed-up is "only if runtime exploits sparsity." Fix: either switch to structured pruning (removes whole channels/filters, benefits standard dense kernels) or use a runtime/library with genuine sparse-matrix support.

bookExercises.prompt: Read the abstract of Han, Mao & Dally's "Deep Compression." Compare its combination of pruning, quantization, and Huffman coding to this chapter's treatment of pruning and quantization as separate, composable techniques. What does combining all three buy over applying either one alone?
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Discussion only. Combining pruning, quantization, and Huffman coding compounds their savings multiplicatively rather than requiring a choice between them. Pruning removes redundant connections, quantization reduces bits per remaining weight, and Huffman coding further compresses the resulting (now more skewed) weight-value distribution losslessly. Applying all three together achieves compression ratios well beyond what any single technique reaches alone, which is the paper's central point.

bookExercises.prompt: A battery-powered soil-moisture sensor needs to report one reading every ten minutes from a location two kilometres from the nearest gateway, with a multi-year battery life target. Using Procedure 64.1's decision heuristic, name the protocol this points to and justify it against the other three.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Procedure 64.1 points to LoRaWAN: it's the only protocol in the comparison combining very-low power (multi-year battery life) with long range (kilometres). MQTT and CoAP don't inherently provide multi-kilometre range without additional network infrastructure, and BLE's range is limited to metres. None of the other three protocols satisfy both the distance and battery-life constraints simultaneously the way LoRaWAN's radio design is specifically built for.
